So the two basic doubts went to Manjula that evening, and the conceptual one was written on a slip to email to the professor before Friday.

Sonali had two kinds of doubts written in her notebook, and she had sorted them on the metro ride to college in Delhi. Column one: small things. Why does this code throw an index error? What's the syntax for reading a file? Column two: big things. Why does this sorting method slow down on nearly sorted data?
Column one isn't for Professor Mathur, she thought. He has two hundred students. Kashish can do those in five minutes.
Kashish, the teaching assistant, ran a help desk in the lab every Tuesday. Sonali went at 2. The index error turned out to be counting from one instead of zero. The file syntax took a minute.
Column two she saved for Thursday's office hours. Professor Mathur spent twenty minutes drawing how the method behaves on nearly sorted data, and said, 'Good question. That's the heart of the topic.'
On the metro home, Sonali ticked both columns.

qa.q: When does Kashish run the help desk?
What was Sonali thinking when she sorted her doubts, and how did she feel about Professor Mathur's time?
qa.a: She felt considerate and a little cautious about using the time of a professor with two hundred students, so she kept small doubts for Kashish.

qa.q: What could Sonali do if Kashish cannot solve a column one doubt?
qa.a: Move it to column two and bring it to office hours, along with what Kashish already tried.

qa.q: How might Professor Mathur see a student who brings only the deep question?
qa.a: He is pleased and engaged, calling it the heart of the topic, since his time goes to real understanding.

grounding: Shows a student sorting doubts, taking basic ones to the teaching assistant and saving the deeper conceptual one for the professor.

'Imran bhai, do you have ten minutes? I have a doubt in thermodynamics.'
'Sure, what is it?'
'Two, actually. First, in this problem, why is the answer in kilojoules when I got joules?'
Imran looked. 'You forgot to divide by a thousand. Units. Done.'
'Okay, that's embarrassing.' Amandeep laughed. 'Second one: why is entropy called a state function if the heat depends on the path?'
Imran rubbed his chin. 'Hmm. I can tell you the rule, but I'm not sure I can explain why properly. That's a Professor Ghosh question.'
'That's what I thought. I didn't want to use up his office hour on units.'
'Smart. Take him the entropy one, and show him your reasoning.'
On Friday, Amandeep did. Professor Ghosh spent twenty minutes on it, drawing two different paths between the same two states, and ended with, 'Hardly anyone asks that. Well done.'

qa.q: What was Amandeep's mistake in the first problem?
qa.a: Amandeep forgot to divide by a thousand.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the first doubt turned out to be units?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a bit embarrassed but laughed it off, relieved it was sorted in seconds.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep bring to Professor Ghosh besides the question?
qa.a: A short note of the reasoning already tried, as Imran suggested, so the professor can see where the thinking stops.

qa.q: How might Imran feel admitting the entropy question was beyond him?
qa.a: Imran seems comfortable being honest about it and glad to point Amandeep to the right person.

grounding: Shows a student taking a basic doubt to a senior and saving a deeper conceptual one for the professor, matching the helper to the problem.
